title: arXivEdits: Understanding the Human Revision Process in Scientific Writing
research_question: How can revisions across successive versions of full scientific papers be aligned, decomposed into fine-grained edits, and automatically classified by the authors' revision intentions?
methodology: The authors construct arXivEdits from 751 multi-version arXiv article groups containing 1,790 versions and manually annotate sentence alignment across 1,039 adjacent-version pairs, including 13,008 candidate sentence pairs. They additionally annotate fine-grained span edits and revision intentions for 1,000 sentence pairs using a seven-category intention taxonomy. Their automatic pipeline performs neural sentence alignment, span-alignment-based edit extraction, and edit-intention classification using models including semi-CRF alignment, QA-Align, PURE, and T5. Performance is measured with alignment F1, edit-extraction precision/recall/F1 and exact match, and intention-classification accuracy and weighted F1.

key_findings.finding: The corpus provides longitudinal full-document revision data for 751 papers and 1,790 versions, with manually annotated sentence alignment covering 13,008 sentence pairs.
The neural sentence-alignment model trained on arXivEdits achieved 93.8 F1, supporting automated linkage of corresponding sentences across document versions.
key_findings.section: Introduction; 4 Automatic Edit Extraction and Intention Identification

key_findings.finding: Span-alignment methods extracted finer-grained edits than latexdiff; QA-align with parse-based heuristics achieved 88.1 F1 on all revisions compared with 75.3 for latexdiff.

A T5-large intention classifier achieved 79.3 accuracy and 78.9 weighted F1 in the fine-grained eight-class experimental setup, while the collapsed four-class setup reached 84.4 accuracy and 84.6 weighted F1 when trained directly on four classes.
The annotated document-level alignments explicitly capture insertions, deletions, rephrasings, splits, merges, fusions, and unchanged copying across successive versions.

limitations: The corpus represents scientific-paper revision rather than workplace messages, tickets, incident reports, or operational work items.
Only 751 of 1,000 randomly selected multi-version article groups yielded complete usable plain text; groups without suitable LaTeX source or with overwhelming mathematical content were excluded.
The alignment procedure skips 5.8% of sentences that are too short or dominated by special tokens, although they remain marked in the dataset.
Fine-grained edit intentions are manually annotated for only 1,000 sentence pairs, much less than the full document-level corpus.
The intention taxonomy describes scientific-writing edits rather than explicit longitudinal operational relations such as supersession, supplementation, reopening, or work-item conflict.
The work does not distinguish an author's assertion that an external task has been completed from independently corroborating evidence of that completion.
raw_claims: arXivEdits follows adjacent versions of the same paper as longitudinal revisions.
The corpus contains 751 complete article groups and 1,790 paper versions.
Crowdworkers annotated sentence correspondence for 13,008 sentence pairs.
The fine-grained subset assigns intentions to span-level insertions, deletions, substitutions, and related edits.
The corpus defines seven semantic categories of revision intention.
Semantic span alignment produces substantially better fine-grained edit extraction than a conventional string-diff baseline.
T5-large is the strongest reported intention classifier in the evaluated configurations.
The released repository contains both data and pipeline code for revision analysis.
